title: Only 7% Pass This Harvard Entrance Exam
summary: Evidence, numbers, priorities and strategic trade-offs test whether your strongest decision survives scrutiny.

landing.intro: Evidence, trade-offs, data and logic collide. Can you make the strongest decision before one overlooked fact changes everything?

about.body:
This independent worldwide-English entertainment challenge uses five increasingly demanding sections to explore reasoning styles associated with university entrance puzzles. It does not reproduce a real Harvard admissions test and requires no university-specific knowledge.

Every question has one answer supported by the information shown. Work at your own pace: speed never affects the score, and the challenge becomes harder through additional reasoning rather than obscure facts.

Your final percentage is the share of 40 puzzles solved correctly. It describes this attempt only and is not an admissions prediction, academic qualification or aptitude assessment.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Use only the information supplied in each question.
Choose one answer per puzzle; correctness remains hidden until the final reveal.
Continue through all five sections, then reveal your entrance score and answer review.

about.disclaimer: Independent entertainment challenge. Not an official Harvard admissions test and not affiliated with any university.

profile-1.title: The Case Room Standout
profile-1.copy: You balanced evidence, numbers and trade-offs with exceptional consistency.

profile-2.title: The Harvard Natural
profile-2.copy: You crossed the challenge line by making clear, evidence-led decisions across very different cases.

profile-3.title: The Strategic Analyst
profile-3.copy: You handled most data and judgement problems strongly, with only a few close calls.

profile-4.title: The Deliberate Thinker
profile-4.copy: You found sound decisions in many cases and built a strong base for another attempt.

profile-5.title: The Promising Applicant
profile-5.copy: Several analytical styles clicked, while the review highlights where one extra comparison mattered.

profile-6.title: The Curious Decision-Maker
profile-6.copy: Some cases proved difficult, but each missed constraint offers a useful lesson for the next decision.

score.passed: You passed the Harvard entrance challenge!

harvard-s1q1.question: A team needs writing, numbers and presentation skills. Which option covers all three with the fewest people?
answers: One writer and one analyst who presents

harvard-s1q2.question: A $250 budget spends 36%. How much remains?

harvard-s1q3.question: Which evidence most directly supports a need for later library hours?
answers: Entry records show repeated turnaways at closing time

harvard-s1q4.question: Two projects have equal benefit. One costs less and finishes sooner. Which should be preferred under those criteria?

harvard-s1q6.question: Applications rise from 400 to 500. What is the percentage increase?

harvard-s1q7.question: A policy benefits 80 people at $4,000. What is its cost per beneficiary?

harvard-s1q8.question: A proposal promises higher participation but gives no mechanism. What is the best first question?
answers: How is the proposal expected to change participation?

harvard-s2q1.question: Which conclusion follows? All funded pilots were reviewed. Project K was funded.

harvard-s2q2.question: A survey of volunteers finds 90% support. What is the biggest limitation?
answers: Volunteers may not represent the whole population

harvard-s2q3.question: Which comparison best tests whether a new reminder increased attendance?
answers: Similar groups with and without the reminder

harvard-s2q4.question: A plan assumes demand will grow. Which evidence most weakens it?
answers: Demand has fallen steadily for four comparable periods

harvard-s2q5.question: A programme serves 60 of 75 applicants. What percentage is served?

harvard-s2q6.question: Which option is an observation rather than an interpretation?

harvard-s2q7.question: A report uses one success story to claim the programme works for everyone. What is the flaw?
answers: One case cannot establish a universal result

harvard-s2q8.question: IMPARTIAL is closest in meaning to…

harvard-s3q1.question: A project costs $18,000 and saves $3,000 per month. After how many months are costs recovered?

harvard-s3q2.question: Three teams process 24 cases each. How many cases in total?

harvard-s3q3.question: A score weights impact twice and feasibility once. Proposal X has impact 8, feasibility 6. What is its total?

harvard-s3q4.question: Project A reaches 120 people for $6,000. Project B reaches 150 for $9,000. Which has lower cost per person?

harvard-s3q5.question: A deadline is fixed. Task X takes 4 days; Y takes 3 and starts after X. Minimum total time?

harvard-s3q6.question: A fund of $12,000 is split 2:1 between programmes A and B. How much goes to A?

harvard-s3q7.question: Which region has the highest success rate?

harvard-s3q8.question: A dashboard shows reach stable, clicks stable, but completed forms fall. Where is the likely problem?

harvard-s4q1.question: Two urgent tasks remain: one prevents immediate harm; the other improves next month's report. Which comes first?

harvard-s4q2.question: A committee must include Finance and Community skills. Ana has Finance; Bo has Community; Cy has both but is unavailable. Smallest available team?

harvard-s4q3.question: A proposal scores impact 7 and cost 4. Another scores impact 8 and cost 8. If higher impact and lower cost are preferred, what is true?

harvard-s4q4.question: A claim says a pilot caused a 10% rise, but the comparison group rose 9%. What is the cautious conclusion?
answers: The pilot had no possible effect
The net difference is small and needs further evidence

harvard-s4q5.question: A project is approved only if value exceeds cost. Value is $45k and cost is $45k. Is it approved?
answers: It depends on the project name
No, because value does not exceed cost

harvard-s4q6.question: Attendance is 200 Monday and 260 Tuesday. What share of the two-day total occurred Tuesday?

harvard-s4q7.question: Which response best acknowledges uncertainty?
answers: The evidence suggests an effect, but the sample is small

harvard-s4q8.question: A decision rule says choose the highest benefit among options under $10k. Which wins?

harvard-s5q1.question: A programme costs $20k, reaches 500 people and achieves 40% completion. What is cost per completion?

harvard-s5q2.question: Every priority project has an owner. Project L has no owner. What follows?
answers: L is not a priority project

harvard-s5q3.question: Proposal A: impact 9, feasibility 5. B: impact 7, feasibility 9. Score = impact + feasibility. Which wins?

harvard-s5q4.question: A survey reports 72% support with a ±4-point margin. Which range matches that uncertainty?

harvard-s5q5.question: A project must be urgent and feasible. X is urgent but not feasible; Y is feasible but not urgent; Z is both. Which qualifies?

harvard-s5q6.question: Region A has 80 successes from 100; B has 117 from 150. Which has the higher rate, and by how much?

harvard-s5q7.question: A pilot's reach rises 20%, but conversion falls from 10% to 8%. Starting from 1,000 people, how do completions change?

harvard-s5q8.question: The final rule selects the lowest-cost proposal scoring at least 15. A: cost 9, score 14. B: cost 12, score 16. C: cost 10, score 15. D: cost 8, score 13. Which is selected?
